blocks.text: The Talmud gives the following characteristics of this animal. The skin is soft (Chulin 122a) and detachable (Sabbat 107a; Tos. s.v. הצרן). It is not dangerous to man, which is why catching or killing it on the Sabbath is forbidden (ibid.). Admittedly these specifications, as already mentioned (§. 272), are too general in nature for the particular species of lizard to be recognized from them; nevertheless, among the many explanations of the Hebrew word, the Arabic translation by حردون [ḥardūn] (Hardsonon) deserves preference, since Hasselquist describes precisely the lizard living in Anatolia, [p. 224] Syria and Eretz Yisrael, and which the lawgiver may well have had in mind. Schwarz (חוצאית הארץ 3, 1) gives the same lizard, but remarks that it is also called al Tsab, which, however, cannot be decisive, since the Arabic name Hardun is beyond doubt.

The aforementioned lizard, on account of its scaly back, is only a kind of chameleon (Rosenmüller loc. cit.), and this latter animal is meant by the זקיתא mentioned in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 108b). Here it is related: “Shem, the son of Noah, said: ‘‘We once suffered much distress, for while we fed the day animals by day and the night animals at night, we did not know what the animal זקיתא was accustomed to eat; then one day I cut a pomegranate into two pieces, out of which a worm fell, which that animal devoured; thereupon I kneaded bran (חיורא*), from which worms came forth, on which the animal lived’’”.
About this animal Mussaphia says: “I believe that it is a wind-snorting animal; some take it for an animal living on wind, for the Targum translates רוח “wind” by זיקא”.

If we add, moreover, that people with a bloated body are called זקאני (A. Sara 31b), we should all the more surely think of the chameleon in our passage. In antiquity the opinion prevailed that this animal lives only on air**); this opinion arose because the chameleon inflates itself and thereby expands so much that its skin becomes almost transparent.
It can go hungry for a long time and feeds on flies, gnats, ants and worms, which it catches with its long sticky tongue.

Conclusion. This animal is also mentioned in the Zohar (Ed. Sulzbach, Paras. Jitro pag. 33); here it is called זקיפא and is [p. 225] identified by the commentary אמרי בינה with the זקיתא mentioned in the preceding §. In the fable related there (which also passed into the קב הישר cap. 83) the זקיטא is depicted as an enemy of snakes, which even defeats the latter. Compare with this Aelian (Thierg. 4, 33), who likewise reports that enmity between the chameleon and the snake. The former, because of its firm skin, does not feel the snake's bites at all; yet the superiority of the chameleon over the snake is not mentioned at all; rather, the former defends itself against the snake by cunning, without which it could become the snake's prey.
Cf., however, on our word the Maarich of Menachem de Lonsano s.v. זקיטא.

Chulin 127a states: Under the צב (toad §. 281), designated by the Law as defiling, are also included the ערוד (water snake §. 300), the סלמנדרא (salamander §. 278) and the בן נפילים. It is the last-named animal that we have to identify here. One should note above all that only with the צב, which belongs to the eight defiling animals, is the addition למינהו “after its kind” (Lev. 11, 29) found, although hardly any of the other seven animals does not also have more or fewer varieties of its genus. How numerous, e.g., is the lizard genus, of which, however, only the לטאה (§. 272) and the כח (§. 274) are mentioned. The Talmud now takes the למינהו attached exclusively to the צב as a collective designation for several other animals, which, however, have in common only that they are all amphibians, since no other prominent common feature could otherwise be found, as the toad, the water snake, the salamander and the skink (בן נפילים) have nothing else in common.

Bochart (l. c. 1, 4, 1), in order to obtain an agreement among the four animals, takes צב for the land crocodile, ערוד (for which he reads עסוד) for a land lizard, בן נפילים for the skink and סלמנדרא for the salamander. But while he correctly identifies the two latter animals, he errs in the two former, since צב in the Talmud means only toad, and no codex has the reading עסוד. If, however, as mentioned, we take the nature of the [p. 226] amphibians as the common feature, there is no further difficulty.

Let us now come to the explanation of our animal. This is, as Buxdorf rightly assumes, a water animal, i.e. an amphibian, which at different times stays now in the water, now on land. He refers (Lex. p. 1368) to the Midrash passage (Rabba Schemoth p. 133), in which it says: God showed Moses many objects so that he might come to know them by sight; He stirred the sea and showed him the בן נפילים u. w.*); from this it follows that the בן נפילים lives in the water. On the other hand, Buxdorf errs, and likewise Landau, who follows him, when the former lets himself be misled by the similarity of sound and translates בן נפילים as Nauplium. He refers to Pliny (h. n. 9, 30, 49), where it says: Mucianus relates that he saw a shell in the form of a ship, and another in the Sea of Marmara, which has a curved stern and in front the prow of a vessel. In this shell the Nauplium is produced; it is similar to a snake and is accustomed to play in company.
